Exponential integrators in NGSolve — Part 1: exponential Euler with Krylov subspaces#

This is the first of four notebooks on exponential integrators for time-dependent finite element problems.

Prerequisites: the NGSolve i-tutorial 3.1 Parabolic model problem (implicit Euler, the mstar trick) and 2.2 Eigenvalue problems (MultiVector).

Why exponential integrators?#

Finite element discretisation of the heat equation \(\partial_t u - \Delta u = f\) with homogeneous Dirichlet data gives the linear system of ODEs

\[ M \dot u(t) + K u(t) = f, \qquad u(0) = u_0, \]

with the mass matrix \(M\) and the stiffness matrix \(K\). Writing \(A := M^{-1}K\) this is \(\dot u = -A u + M^{-1} f\), and the exact solution over one time step \(\Delta t\) is

\[ u(t_{n+1}) = e^{-\Delta t A}\, u(t_n) + \Delta t\, \varphi_1(-\Delta t A)\, M^{-1} f, \qquad \varphi_1(z) = \frac{e^z - 1}{z}. \]

Every classical time stepping method replaces the matrix exponential by a rational function: implicit Euler uses \((1+z)^{-1} \approx e^{-z}\), Crank–Nicolson uses \((1-z/2)/(1+z/2)\). The price is a time discretisation error of order \(\Delta t\) or \(\Delta t^2\). The problem is stiff: the eigenvalues of \(A\) range from \(\lambda_{\min} \approx 2\pi^2\) up to \(\lambda_{\max} \sim h^{-2}\), so explicit methods are useless and even A-stable methods like Crank–Nicolson damp the unresolved high-frequency modes incorrectly.

Exponential integrators apply \(e^{-\Delta t A}\) (and \(\varphi_1\)) exactly up to a tolerance we choose. For the linear problem above the time discretisation error disappears completely; for nonlinear or time-dependent problems (Parts 3 and 4) it is reduced to the treatment of the nonlinearity. Of course we never form the matrix \(e^{-\Delta t A}\): it is dense. What we need is its action on a vector, \(v \mapsto e^{-\Delta t A} v\), and this is what Krylov subspace methods deliver with a few sparse matrix–vector products or sparse solves.

The only NGSolve ingredients are MultiVector.AppendOrthogonalize (one step of Gram–Schmidt in the mass matrix inner product) and a sparse factorisation via Inverse. Nothing has to be added to the C++ core.

from ngsolve import *
from ngsolve.webgui import Draw
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg as sla
import scipy.sparse as sp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from time import time as walltime
ngsglobals.msg_level = 0

Model problem#

Unit square, homogeneous Dirichlet conditions on the whole boundary, \(H^1\) elements of order 3. As in tutorial 3.1 we assemble mass and stiffness matrices separately. We assemble with symmetric=False so that both matrices have the same (full) sparsity pattern — this lets us form linear combinations like \(M + \gamma K\) entry-wise later, and it makes the export to scipy via COO() complete (a symmetric matrix would only export its lower triangle).

mesh = Mesh(unit_square.GenerateMesh(maxh=0.07))
fes = H1(mesh, order=3, dirichlet=".*")
u, v = fes.TnT()

a = BilinearForm(grad(u)*grad(v)*dx, symmetric=False).Assemble()   # stiffness K
m = BilinearForm(u*v*dx, symmetric=False).Assemble()               # mass M
K, M = a.mat, m.mat

f = LinearForm(fes)
f += 1*v*dx                                                        # constant source
f.Assemble()

freedofs = fes.FreeDofs()
P = Projector(freedofs, True)     # sets the Dirichlet dofs of a vector to zero
print(f"ndof = {fes.ndof},  free dofs = {sum(freedofs)}")

ndof = 2200,  free dofs = 2032

As initial datum we take a rough function — a Gaussian plus a jump — so that all frequencies are present. Note the projection P: Set also fills the Dirichlet dofs, but our ODE lives on the free dofs only. All vectors that enter a Krylov method below must be zero on the Dirichlet dofs, otherwise the mass matrix inner product couples them to the boundary and the iteration diverges.

u0 = exp(-100*((x-0.3)**2 + (y-0.6)**2)) + IfPos((x-0.5)*(0.8-x), 1, 0)*IfPos((y-0.2)*(0.5-y), 1, 0)
gfu = GridFunction(fes)
gfu.Set(u0)
gfu.vec.data = P * gfu.vec
u0vec = gfu.vec.CreateVector(); u0vec.data = gfu.vec      # keep a copy of the initial datum
Draw(gfu, mesh, "u0");

Reference: the \(\theta\)-scheme (implicit Euler, Crank–Nicolson)#

\[ (M + \theta \Delta t K)\, u^{n+1} = (M - (1-\theta)\Delta t K)\, u^n + \Delta t\, f, \qquad \theta = 1 \text{ (implicit Euler)},\quad \theta = \tfrac12 \text{ (Crank–Nicolson)}. \]

One sparse factorisation of \(M^\ast = M + \theta \Delta t K\) serves for all time steps. We build \(M^\ast\) with the AsVector trick of tutorial 3.1.

def ThetaScheme(theta, dt):
    "returns a function performing one step of the theta-scheme"
    mstar = M.CreateMatrix()
    mstar.AsVector().data = M.AsVector() + theta*dt * K.AsVector()
    inv = mstar.Inverse(freedofs, inverse="sparsecholesky")
    def step(uvec):
        return (inv * (M*uvec - (1-theta)*dt*(K*uvec) + dt*f.vec)).Evaluate()
    return step

The exact solution and the stiffness of \(A\)#

\(A = M^{-1}K\) is not symmetric, but it is self-adjoint with respect to the mass matrix inner product \((u,v)_M = v^T M u\):

\[ (Au, v)_M = v^T M M^{-1} K u = v^T K u = (u, Av)_M . \]

Hence \(A\) has real positive eigenvalues \(\lambda_k\) with \(M\)-orthonormal eigenvectors \(w_k\) (\(K w_k = \lambda_k M w_k\), \(W^T M W = I\)), and

\[ e^{-\Delta t A} v = W\, \mathrm{diag}(e^{-\Delta t \lambda_k})\, W^T M v . \]

Every mode is damped by exactly \(e^{-\Delta t\lambda_k}\). On our coarse mesh we can afford the dense generalised eigenproblem with scipy — only as a reference; for real problems this is impossible and Krylov methods are the way to go. The \(M\)-norm \(\|v\|_M = \sqrt{v^T M v}\) is the \(L^2\) norm of the finite element function; all errors below are measured in it.

idx = np.array([i for i in range(fes.ndof) if freedofs[i]])       # free dofs

def dense_free(mat):
    "dense matrix restricted to the free dofs (needs symmetric=False assembly!)"
    r, c, val = mat.COO()
    return sp.csr_matrix((val, (r, c)), shape=(mat.height, mat.width)).toarray()[np.ix_(idx, idx)]

Kd, Md = dense_free(K), dense_free(M)
lam, W = sla.eigh(Kd, Md)               # K W = M W diag(lam),  W^T M W = I
print(f"lambda_min = {lam[0]:.3f}  (exact 2 pi^2 = {2*pi**2:.3f}),   lambda_max = {lam[-1]:.3e}")

def to_np(vec):           return np.array(vec.FV().NumPy())[idx]
def norm_M(vnp):          return sqrt(vnp @ (Md @ vnp))
def exact_funm(func, vnp): return W @ (func(lam) * (W.T @ (Md @ vnp)))       # f(A) v
def relerr(vec, ref_np):  return norm_M(to_np(vec) - ref_np) / norm_M(ref_np)

lambda_min = 19.739  (exact 2 pi^2 = 19.739),   lambda_max = 7.891e+04

For \(\Delta t = 0.01\) the stiffness ratio \(\Delta t\,\lambda_{\max}\) is a few hundred: the highest modes are damped by \(e^{-800} \approx 0\) while the lowest one only by \(e^{-0.2}\). This ratio is what makes the matrix exponential hard to approximate by polynomials.

dt = 0.01
print(f"dt*lambda_max = {dt*lam[-1]:.0f},   dt*lambda_min = {dt*lam[0]:.3f}")
u0np  = to_np(u0vec)
ref_exp = exact_funm(lambda l: np.exp(-dt*l), u0np)       # exact e^{-dt A} u0

dt*lambda_max = 789,   dt*lambda_min = 0.197

Krylov approximation of \(f(A)\,v\)#

The Krylov space \(\mathcal K_m(A, v) = \mathrm{span}\{v, Av, \dots, A^{m-1}v\}\) contains all polynomials of degree \(< m\) in \(A\) applied to \(v\). Lanczos’ algorithm builds an \(M\)-orthonormal basis \(V_m = [v_1, \dots, v_m]\) of it, \(V_m^T M V_m = I\), together with the small symmetric tridiagonal matrix

\[ T_m = V_m^T M A V_m \in \mathbb R^{m\times m}, \qquad A V_m = V_m T_m + t_{m+1,m}\, v_{m+1} e_m^T . \]

\(T_m\) is the projection of \(A\) onto the Krylov space, and the classical approximation (Saad 1992, Hochbruck–Lubich 1997) is

\[ f(A)\, v \;\approx\; \beta\, V_m\, f(T_m)\, e_1, \qquad \beta = \|v\|_M . \]

\(f(T_m)\) is a small dense matrix function which we evaluate exactly through the eigendecomposition of \(T_m\) (never through inv(T)). The approximation is exact if \(f\) is a polynomial of degree \(< m\); the error is governed by how well \(f\) can be approximated by such polynomials on the spectrum of \(A\).

One step of the Lanczos/Arnoldi process is exactly what NGSolve’s MultiVector.AppendOrthogonalize(w, ipmat=M) does: it \(M\)-orthogonalises the new vector \(w = A v_j\) against the existing basis (two passes of modified Gram–Schmidt — cheap insurance against loss of orthogonality), appends the normalised remainder as \(v_{j+1}\), and returns the coefficients \((t_{0j}, \dots, t_{j+1,j})\), i.e. one column of \(T_m\).

As stopping criterion we use the change of the approximation between two consecutive Krylov dimensions — since \(V_m\) is \(M\)-orthonormal this is just the Euclidean norm of the difference of the coefficient vectors \(\beta f(T_m)e_1\). (Saad’s residual estimate \(\beta\, t_{m+1,m} |e_m^T f(T_m) e_1|\) is discussed in Part 2.) We first write the helpers; the class wrapping them for time stepping follows below.

from math import factorial

def phi(k, z):
    "phi_k(z) for numpy arrays, stable near 0:  phi_0 = exp,  phi_{k+1}(z) = (phi_k(z) - 1/k!)/z"
    z = np.asarray(z); out = np.zeros(z.shape, dtype=np.result_type(z, float))
    with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        small = np.abs(z) < 0.5
        s = np.zeros_like(z[small], dtype=out.dtype)
        for j in range(19, -1, -1):                       # Taylor series sum_j z^j/(j+k)!
            s = s*z[small] + 1.0/factorial(j+k)
        out[small] = s
        p = np.exp(z[~small])
        for i in range(k):
            p = (p - 1.0/factorial(i)) / z[~small]
        out[~small] = p
    return np.where(np.isfinite(out), out, 0.0)         # z = -inf -> 0

def funm_small_sym(T, func):
    "func(T) e_1 for a small symmetric matrix T via its eigendecomposition"
    th, Q = sla.eigh(0.5*(T + T.T))
    return Q @ (func(th) * Q[0, :])

def krylov_funm(op, M, v, func, maxm=60, tol=1e-8, info=None):
    "approximate func(op) v by Lanczos in the M-inner product; op: BaseVector -> BaseVector, M-selfadjoint"
    beta = sqrt(InnerProduct(v, M*v))
    if beta == 0.0:
        return (0.0*v).Evaluate()
    V = MultiVector(v, 0)
    V.Append((1.0/beta) * v)
    T = np.zeros((maxm+1, maxm))
    Eold, hist = np.zeros(0), []
    for j in range(maxm):
        h = np.array(V.AppendOrthogonalize(op(V[j]), ipmat=M)).ravel()   # one Lanczos step
        T[:j+2, j] = h[:j+2]
        E = beta * funm_small_sym(T[:j+1, :j+1], func)                    # coefficients w.r.t. V
        diff = np.linalg.norm(E - np.append(Eold, np.zeros(j+1-len(Eold))))
        hist.append(diff); Eold = E
        if h[j+1] < 1e-14*abs(h).max() or (j >= 1 and diff < tol*beta):   # invariant subspace / converged
            break
    m = len(E)
    if info is not None:
        info["m"], info["hist"] = m, hist
    return (V[0:m] * Vector(E)).Evaluate()

(a) Polynomial Krylov: \(A = M^{-1}K\)#

Each Lanczos step needs one product with \(K\) and one solve with the mass matrix (a sparse Cholesky factorisation of \(M\), computed once). Let us watch the error against the exact \(e^{-\Delta t A}u_0\) as the Krylov dimension \(m\) grows.

invM = M.Inverse(freedofs, inverse="sparsecholesky")
tmp = M.CreateColVector()
def opA(z):                                # z -> M^{-1} K z
    out = M.CreateColVector(); tmp.data = K*z; out.data = invM*tmp; return out

ms_poly, errs_poly = [10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100], []
for mm in ms_poly:
    yk = krylov_funm(opA, M, u0vec, lambda th: np.exp(-dt*th), maxm=mm, tol=0)
    errs_poly.append(relerr(yk, ref_exp))
    print(f"polynomial Krylov  m = {mm:3d}   rel. error = {errs_poly[-1]:.2e}")

polynomial Krylov  m =  10   rel. error = 5.91e-01
polynomial Krylov  m =  20   rel. error = 3.00e-01
polynomial Krylov  m =  40   rel. error = 3.18e-02
polynomial Krylov  m =  60   rel. error = 1.35e-03

polynomial Krylov  m =  80   rel. error = 2.04e-05

polynomial Krylov  m = 100   rel. error = 1.15e-07

Convergence sets in only after roughly \(m \approx \sqrt{\Delta t\,\lambda_{\max}}\) steps (Hochbruck–Lubich 1997) and hence deteriorates under mesh refinement like \(h^{-1}\). That is fine for mildly stiff problems, but for a fine mesh in 3D we would need hundreds of \(M\)-orthogonal basis vectors per time step.

(b) Shift-and-invert (rational) Krylov#

The remedy (van den Eshof–Hochbruck 2006, Moret–Novati 2004) is to build the Krylov space not with \(A\) but with the resolvent

\[ B = (I + \gamma A)^{-1} = (M + \gamma K)^{-1} M , \qquad \gamma > 0 . \]

\(B\) has the same eigenvectors as \(A\), with eigenvalues \(\theta_k = 1/(1+\gamma\lambda_k) \in (0, 1]\): the unbounded spectrum of \(A\) is squeezed into a bounded interval, and the stiff modes (\(\lambda_k\) large) are all mapped close to \(\theta = 0\), where \(e^{-\Delta t\lambda}\) is essentially zero anyway. We run the same Lanczos process with \(B\) and evaluate

\[ e^{-\Delta t A} v \approx \beta V_m\, g(\tilde T_m)\, e_1, \qquad g(\theta) = \exp\Big(-\Delta t\, \frac{1/\theta - 1}{\gamma}\Big), \]

i.e. we simply compose the eigenvalue map \(\lambda = (1/\theta - 1)/\gamma\) with the exponential. Each Lanczos step now costs one product with \(M\) and one back-substitution with the factorisation of \(M + \gamma K\) — the same matrix as for implicit Euler with step \(\gamma\). The convergence is independent of the mesh size and of \(\Delta t\); the rule of thumb \(\gamma \approx \Delta t/10\) is good for tolerances around \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-8}\).

gamma = 0.1*dt
mstar = M.CreateMatrix()
mstar.AsVector().data = M.AsVector() + gamma*K.AsVector()
invmstar = mstar.Inverse(freedofs, inverse="sparsecholesky")
def opB(z):                                # z -> (M + gamma K)^{-1} M z
    out = M.CreateColVector(); tmp.data = M*z; out.data = invmstar*tmp; return out

def g_exp(th):                             # exp(-dt lambda) with lambda = (1/theta - 1)/gamma
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
        return np.exp(-dt * np.where(th > 0, (1/th - 1)/gamma, np.inf))

ms_si, errs_si = [4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24], []
for mm in ms_si:
    yk = krylov_funm(opB, M, u0vec, g_exp, maxm=mm, tol=0)
    errs_si.append(relerr(yk, ref_exp))
    print(f"shift-and-invert Krylov  m = {mm:3d}   rel. error = {errs_si[-1]:.2e}")

shift-and-invert Krylov  m =   4   rel. error = 9.81e-02
shift-and-invert Krylov  m =   8   rel. error = 5.63e-04
shift-and-invert Krylov  m =  12   rel. error = 3.69e-06
shift-and-invert Krylov  m =  16   rel. error = 7.07e-08
shift-and-invert Krylov  m =  20   rel. error = 2.17e-09
shift-and-invert Krylov  m =  24   rel. error = 9.98e-11

Two dozen sparse back-substitutions give the matrix exponential to ten digits. Let us also check that the built-in stopping estimate (change between consecutive iterates) is a faithful indicator of the true error: it typically lags the true error by one iteration, so a tolerance tol gives an error of roughly tol or slightly better.

info = {}
yk = krylov_funm(opB, M, u0vec, g_exp, maxm=40, tol=1e-12, info=info)
true_err = [relerr(krylov_funm(opB, M, u0vec, g_exp, maxm=mm, tol=0), ref_exp) for mm in range(1, info["m"]+1)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
ax[0].semilogy(ms_poly, errs_poly, "o-", label="polynomial Krylov, $A=M^{-1}K$")
ax[0].semilogy(ms_si, errs_si, "s-", label=r"shift-and-invert, $B=(M+\gamma K)^{-1}M$")
ax[0].set_xlabel("Krylov dimension m"); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"rel. error in $\|\cdot\|_M$"); ax[0].legend(); ax[0].grid()
ax[0].set_title(rf"$e^{{-\Delta t A}}u_0$,  $\Delta t\,\lambda_{{max}}$ = {dt*lam[-1]:.0f}")
ax[1].semilogy(range(1, info["m"]+1), true_err, "s-", label="true error")
ax[1].semilogy(range(1, info["m"]+1), np.array(info["hist"])/sqrt(InnerProduct(u0vec, M*u0vec)), "x--", label="estimate (change of iterate)")
ax[1].set_xlabel("Krylov dimension m"); ax[1].legend(); ax[1].grid(); ax[1].set_title("shift-and-invert: error estimator")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The exponential Euler method#

We now have everything for the exact step

\[ u^{n+1} = e^{-\Delta t A} u^n + \Delta t\, \varphi_1(-\Delta t A)\, M^{-1} f . \]

The \(\varphi_1\)-term is obtained from the same Krylov routine: only the scalar function changes (\(g(\theta) = \varphi_1(-\Delta t\lambda(\theta))\)). For a constant source it is a fixed vector and computed once.

To make the time loop look like the one of tutorial 3.1 we wrap the Krylov exponential into a BaseMatrix: then E * u is the action of \(e^{-\Delta t A}\), and E.Phi(1, w) the action of \(\varphi_1(-\Delta t A)\). (The class is also available as expint_tools.KrylovExp, together with the polynomial variant and an Arnoldi version for non-symmetric operators used in Part 3.)

class KrylovExp(BaseMatrix):
    "y = exp(-dt A) x,  A = M^{-1} K on the free dofs, by shift-and-invert Lanczos with B = (M + gamma K)^{-1} M"
    def __init__(self, M, K, dt, freedofs, gamma=None, tol=1e-8, maxm=60):
        super().__init__()
        self.M, self.dt, self.tol, self.maxm, self.info = M, dt, tol, maxm, {}
        self.gamma = 0.1*dt if gamma is None else gamma
        self.P = Projector(freedofs, True)
        mstar = M.CreateMatrix()
        mstar.AsVector().data = M.AsVector() + self.gamma*K.AsVector()
        self.inv = mstar.Inverse(freedofs, inverse="sparsecholesky")
        self.tmp = M.CreateColVector()

    def Height(self):         return self.M.height
    def Width(self):          return self.M.width
    def IsComplex(self):      return False
    def CreateRowVector(self): return self.M.CreateRowVector()
    def CreateColVector(self): return self.M.CreateColVector()

    def op(self, z):                                    # z -> B z
        out = self.M.CreateColVector(); self.tmp.data = self.M*z; out.data = self.inv*self.tmp; return out

    def Apply(self, x, func):                           # func(A) x  for a scalar function func(lambda)
        def g(th):
            with np.errstate(divide="ignore", over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
                return func(np.where(th > 0, (1/th - 1)/self.gamma, np.inf))
        xp = self.M.CreateColVector(); xp.data = self.P*x
        return krylov_funm(self.op, self.M, xp, g, self.maxm, self.tol, self.info)

    def Mult(self, x, y):   y.data = self.Apply(x, lambda lam: np.exp(-self.dt*lam))
    def Phi(self, k, x):    return self.Apply(x, lambda lam: phi(k, -self.dt*lam))

The time loop. Compare with tutorial 3.1: there the step was gfu.vec.data += invmstar * res; here it is gfu.vec.data = E * gfu.vec + g with \(g = \Delta t\,\varphi_1(-\Delta t A) M^{-1} f\). We record the Krylov dimension used in each step.

def ExpEuler(dt, tend, tol=1e-8, nsamples=20):
    E = KrylovExp(M, K, dt, freedofs, tol=tol)
    g = dt * E.Phi(1, invM*f.vec)                     # constant source: once
    gfu.Set(u0); gfu.vec.data = P*gfu.vec
    gfut = GridFunction(fes, multidim=0); gfut.AddMultiDimComponent(gfu.vec)
    nsteps = int(round(tend/dt)); ms = []
    for n in range(nsteps):
        gfu.vec.data = E*gfu.vec + g
        ms.append(E.info["m"])
        if (n+1) % max(1, nsteps//nsamples) == 0:
            gfut.AddMultiDimComponent(gfu.vec)
    print(f"{nsteps} steps of size {dt}: Krylov dimension per step between {min(ms)} and {max(ms)}")
    return gfut

t0 = walltime()
gfut = ExpEuler(dt=0.01, tend=0.5)
print(f"wall time {walltime()-t0:.2f} s")
Draw(gfut, mesh, interpolate_multidim=True, animate=True, min=0, max=0.4);

50 steps of size 0.01: Krylov dimension per step between 14 and 19
wall time 0.25 s

Accuracy versus \(\Delta t\)#

We compare implicit Euler, Crank–Nicolson and the exponential Euler method on smooth compatible data, \(u_0 = f = \sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)\), against the exact solution of the semi-discrete problem at \(T = 0.2\),

\[ u(T) = e^{-TA}u_0 + T\,\varphi_1(-TA)\,M^{-1}f = W\Big(e^{-T\Lambda} W^T M u_0 + \tfrac{1 - e^{-T\Lambda}}{\Lambda} W^T f\Big). \]
fs = LinearForm(fes); fs += sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)*v*dx; fs.Assemble()
gfs = GridFunction(fes); gfs.Set(sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)); gfs.vec.data = P*gfs.vec
Tend = 0.2
exact_T = exact_funm(lambda l: np.exp(-Tend*l), to_np(gfs.vec)) + W @ ((1 - np.exp(-Tend*lam))/lam * (W.T @ to_np(fs.vec)))

def run_theta(theta, dt, uinit, fvec):
    mstar = M.CreateMatrix(); mstar.AsVector().data = M.AsVector() + theta*dt*K.AsVector()
    inv = mstar.Inverse(freedofs, inverse="sparsecholesky")
    w = uinit.CreateVector(); w.data = uinit
    for n in range(int(round(Tend/dt))):
        w.data = inv * (M*w - (1-theta)*dt*(K*w) + dt*fvec)
    return w

def run_expeuler(dt, uinit, fvec, tol=1e-8):
    E = KrylovExp(M, K, dt, freedofs, tol=tol)
    g = dt * E.Phi(1, invM*fvec)
    w = uinit.CreateVector(); w.data = uinit
    for n in range(int(round(Tend/dt))):
        w.data = E*w + g
    return w

dts = [0.04, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005, 0.0025]
err = {"implicit Euler": [], "Crank-Nicolson": [], "exponential Euler": []}
for dt_ in dts:
    err["implicit Euler"].append(relerr(run_theta(1.0, dt_, gfs.vec, fs.vec), exact_T))
    err["Crank-Nicolson"].append(relerr(run_theta(0.5, dt_, gfs.vec, fs.vec), exact_T))
    err["exponential Euler"].append(relerr(run_expeuler(dt_, gfs.vec, fs.vec), exact_T))

print(f"{'dt':>8s} " + " ".join(f"{k:>18s}" for k in err))
for i, dt_ in enumerate(dts):
    print(f"{dt_:8.4f} " + " ".join(f"{err[k][i]:18.2e}" for k in err))
for k in ["implicit Euler", "Crank-Nicolson"]:
    print(f"estimated order {k}: {np.log2(err[k][-2]/err[k][-1]):.2f}")

plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 3.8))
for k, e in err.items(): plt.loglog(dts, e, "o-", label=k)
plt.loglog(dts, [d/dts[0]*err["implicit Euler"][0] for d in dts], "k:", lw=.8, label=r"$O(\Delta t)$")
plt.loglog(dts, [(d/dts[0])**2*err["Crank-Nicolson"][0] for d in dts], "k--", lw=.8, label=r"$O(\Delta t^2)$")
plt.xlabel(r"$\Delta t$"); plt.ylabel("rel. error at T=0.2"); plt.legend(); plt.grid(); plt.show()

      dt     implicit Euler     Crank-Nicolson  exponential Euler
  0.0400           4.84e-01           5.39e-02           2.19e-09
  0.0200           2.28e-01           1.36e-02           2.94e-09
  0.0100           1.09e-01           3.40e-03           3.58e-09
  0.0050           5.33e-02           8.51e-04           4.43e-09
  0.0025           2.63e-02           2.13e-04           4.80e-09

The exponential Euler error is independent of \(\Delta t\) and equal to the Krylov tolerance: the time discretisation error is gone. Even better, the number of steps does not matter; for a linear problem with constant source one can take \(\Delta t = T\) and be done in a single step.

Remark: Crank–Nicolson and rough data. Repeat the experiment with the rough initial datum from above and \(f = 1\). Crank–Nicolson is A-stable, but its stability function \(R(z) = (1+z/2)/(1-z/2)\) tends to \(-1\) for \(z \to -\infty\): unresolved high-frequency modes are not damped, they oscillate with amplitude one. Exponential integrators inherit the exact damping \(e^{-\Delta t\lambda}\) of every mode.

exact_T_rough = exact_funm(lambda l: np.exp(-Tend*l), u0np) + W @ ((1 - np.exp(-Tend*lam))/lam * (W.T @ to_np(f.vec)))
print(f"{'dt':>8s} {'implicit Euler':>16s} {'Crank-Nicolson':>16s} {'exp. Euler':>16s}")
for dt_ in dts:
    e1 = relerr(run_theta(1.0, dt_, u0vec, f.vec), exact_T_rough)
    e2 = relerr(run_theta(0.5, dt_, u0vec, f.vec), exact_T_rough)
    e3 = relerr(run_expeuler(dt_, u0vec, f.vec), exact_T_rough)
    print(f"{dt_:8.4f} {e1:16.2e} {e2:16.2e} {e3:16.2e}")

      dt   implicit Euler   Crank-Nicolson       exp. Euler
  0.0400         1.12e-01         2.59e+00         7.92e-10
  0.0200         5.27e-02         1.75e+00         1.52e-09

  0.0100         2.52e-02         1.01e+00         3.82e-09

  0.0050         1.23e-02         3.96e-01         1.99e-09

  0.0025         6.05e-03         4.54e-02         2.54e-09

Cost#

Per time step the shift-and-invert method needs \(m\) back-substitutions with the factorisation of \(M + \gamma K\) plus \(m\) products with \(M\) and the Gram–Schmidt work, compared to one back-substitution for implicit Euler. With \(m \approx 15\)–\(30\) this looks like a factor 20 — but implicit Euler needs \(\Delta t \approx 10^{-6}\) (thousands of steps) to reach the accuracy the exponential method delivers in one step of any size. Here is the same computation as above (\(T = 0.5\), constant \(f\)) in one step:

t0 = walltime()
E = KrylovExp(M, K, 0.5, freedofs, tol=1e-10)
uT = (E*u0vec + 0.5*E.Phi(1, invM*f.vec)).Evaluate()
t1 = walltime() - t0
ex05 = exact_funm(lambda l: np.exp(-0.5*l), u0np) + W @ ((1 - np.exp(-0.5*lam))/lam * (W.T @ to_np(f.vec)))
print(f"one exponential Euler step to T=0.5:  {t1:.3f} s,  Krylov dim {E.info['m']},  rel. error {relerr(uT, ex05):.1e}")

for dt_, nsteps in [(1e-2, 50), (1e-3, 500), (1e-4, 5000)]:
    t0 = walltime()
    step = ThetaScheme(1.0, dt_); w = u0vec.CreateVector(); w.data = u0vec
    for n in range(nsteps): w.data = step(w)
    print(f"{nsteps:5d} implicit Euler steps (dt={dt_:.0e}) to T=0.5:  {walltime()-t0:.3f} s,  rel. error {relerr(w, ex05):.1e}")

one exponential Euler step to T=0.5:  0.011 s,  Krylov dim 9,  rel. error 8.0e-11
   50 implicit Euler steps (dt=1e-02) to T=0.5:  0.016 s,  rel. error 2.4e-04
  500 implicit Euler steps (dt=1e-03) to T=0.5:  0.128 s,  rel. error 1.8e-05

 5000 implicit Euler steps (dt=1e-04) to T=0.5:  1.261 s,  rel. error 1.7e-06

Tests#

The following assertions document the expected behaviour (they also run in the test suite tests/test_expint.py).

# (i) a single eigenmode decays like exp(-2 pi^2 t); the error is the p=3 discretisation error
gfe = GridFunction(fes); gfe.Set(sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)); gfe.vec.data = P*gfe.vec
E = KrylovExp(M, K, 0.01, freedofs, tol=1e-10)
for n in range(10): gfe.vec.data = E*gfe.vec
err_mode = sqrt(Integrate((gfe - exp(-2*pi**2*0.1)*sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y))**2, mesh))
print(f"eigenmode test: L2 error {err_mode:.2e},  Krylov dim {E.info['m']}")
assert err_mode < 1e-5 and E.info["m"] <= 6

# (ii) rough data: Krylov approximations converge to the dense reference
assert errs_poly[-1] < 1e-6 and errs_si[-1] < 1e-8 and min(true_err) < 1e-10

# (iii) phi_1 against the dense reference
Minvf = (invM*f.vec).Evaluate()
g1 = KrylovExp(M, K, dt, freedofs, tol=1e-10).Phi(1, Minvf)
assert relerr(g1, exact_funm(lambda l: phi(1, -dt*l), to_np(Minvf))) < 1e-8

# (iv) orders of the time stepping methods
assert 0.8 < np.log2(err["implicit Euler"][-2]/err["implicit Euler"][-1]) < 1.2
assert 1.8 < np.log2(err["Crank-Nicolson"][-2]/err["Crank-Nicolson"][-1]) < 2.2
assert max(err["exponential Euler"]) < 1e-6
print("all tests passed")

eigenmode test: L2 error 1.19e-07,  Krylov dim 3
all tests passed

Summary and outlook#

  • The exact solution of the semi-discrete heat equation is \(u^{n+1} = e^{-\Delta t A}u^n + \Delta t\varphi_1(-\Delta t A)M^{-1}f\) with \(A = M^{-1}K\).

  • \(A\) is self-adjoint in the \(M\)-inner product; Krylov methods must use this inner product (AppendOrthogonalize(..., ipmat=M)).

  • Polynomial Krylov needs \(m \sim \sqrt{\Delta t\,\lambda_{\max}}\) steps; shift-and-invert Krylov with one factorisation of \(M + \gamma K\), \(\gamma \approx \Delta t/10\), converges in 10–30 steps independently of the mesh.

  • The \(\varphi\)-functions come from the same routine with a different scalar function.

Part 2 compares these Krylov methods with Chebyshev expansions, scipy’s expm_multiply, and contour integrals (rational approximations with complex shifts), and looks at error estimators and the choice of \(\gamma\). Part 3 treats non-symmetric operators (convection–diffusion, Arnoldi instead of Lanczos) and time-dependent sources (exponential Runge–Kutta methods of order 2). Part 4 applies exponential Euler and exponential Rosenbrock–Euler to the nonlinear Allen–Cahn equation.
